169.title: The example of the wise (3.17–3.29)
169.hook: people copy what you do, not what you say, and Krishna says even he keeps working for that reason
169.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often cite Gita 3.20–3.21, on lokasangraha and on people following the example of the best, when speaking of leadership, parenting and public service, and King Janaka is remembered as the model of a wise person who kept working in the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wheel of sacrifice: food, rain, offering, action, and the one who only takes. Your line was give back. What did you hand on? Today, who's watching you turn the wheel. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

If you've ever been around a small child for more than a day, you know. They don't do what you tell them. They do what you do. You say be gentle, and then you slam the cupboard, and guess which one they learn. The same is true in offices, teams, families, whole countries. People watch the person at the front, and they copy. Krishna has just told Arjuna to work as an offering. Now he adds a reason Arjuna hadn't thought of. Even if you didn't need to act, other people need you to.
screen: `THEY DO WHAT YOU DO.` → `PEOPLE WATCH THE ONE IN FRONT.` → `OTHERS NEED YOU TO ACT.`

segments.voice: Krishna begins with the rare person who's already free: someone who delights in the self, is content in the self, has nothing left they need to do. You'd think that person could stop. But, Krishna says, look at King Janaka. Janaka was a ruler famous for his wisdom, a sage who never left his throne, and he and others like him reached perfection through action. Then the word for why: lokasangraham evapi sampashyan kartum arhasi. Keeping in view the holding-together of the world, you should act. Lokasangraha: the good of the world, the keeping of people together. Then the famous line. Yad yad acharati shreshthas tat tad evetaro janah. Whatever the best person does, others do the same. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. And here Krishna points at himself. There's nothing in all three worlds I have to do, he says, nothing I lack and need to get. And yet I keep acting. Because if I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart. So, he says, the wise should act as eagerly as the attached do, but unattached, for the good of the world. And they shouldn't unsettle simpler people who are attached to their work; they should do the work well beside them. One more turn at the end. All actions are carried out by the qualities of nature, the gunas. Only the one confused by ego thinks, I am the doer: ahankara vimudhatma kartaham iti manyate. The wise lead by example, and they don't take the credit.
screen: `JANAKA: A SAGE WHO KEPT HIS THRONE.` · `LOKASANGRAHA: HOLD THE WORLD TOGETHER.` · `WHATEVER THE BEST DO, OTHERS DO.` · `EVEN KRISHNA KEEPS WORKING.` · then, large: `LEAD BY DOING, NOT BY TAKING CREDIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see who's watching. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people who see you most: a child, a younger sibling, a coworker, a friend who's struggling, even a stranger on your usual bus. Let their faces come one by one. Now ask, gently: if they copied exactly what I did yesterday, not what I said, what would they learn? Don't judge it. Just see it. Then pick one small thing you'd be glad for them to copy, and picture yourself doing it in front of them tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
The example of the wise. Whatever the best person does, others do. So even the free keep working, for the good of the world.
screen: `THE EXAMPLE OF THE WISE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: lead by doing. Today, do the thing you keep telling other people to do, where they can see it, and don't mention it. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

what it means: people copy what the best do, so even the free keep working, for the world's sake, without thinking I am the doer.
what a scholar hears: lokasangraha, 'holding the world together', became a key word for modern Hindu thinkers of public service, from Tilak to Gandhi.

170.title: Desire as the enemy (3.30–3.43)
170.hook: Arjuna asks why people do what they know is wrong, as if pushed by force, and Krishna names the enemy
170.howItsDone: Gita 3.35, better one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well, and 3.37, naming desire and anger as the enemy, are verses some Hindus learn by heart and return to when facing a hard choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the example of the wise: whatever the best do, others do, so even Krishna keeps working. Your line was lead by doing. What did someone see you do? Today, the end of chapter three. Day one hundred seventy.

Ten minutes after the text someone swore they wouldn't send, a small question shows up: why did I do that? I knew better. The same question follows the third helping, the thing said in anger, the app opened again at midnight. It's as if something else had its hands on the wheel. Near the end of chapter three, Arjuna asks exactly this. What pushes a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against their own will, as if forced? Krishna's answer is short, and it names two things.
screen: `WHY DID I DO THAT?` → `SOMETHING ELSE AT THE WHEEL.` → `ARJUNA ASKS IT TOO.`

segments.voice: First Krishna gathers up the chapter. Offer all your actions to me, he says, and fight free of fever. Then verse thirty-five. Shreyan svadharmo vigunah, paradharmat svanushthitat. Better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Do your own work, even clumsily; someone else's path, however well walked, is full of fear. Then Arjuna's question, in Sanskrit: atha kena prayukto 'yam papam charati purushah. Then, by what is a person driven to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? And Krishna's answer: kama esha krodha esha. It is desire. It is anger. Born of restlessness, the quality called rajas. All-devouring, and the great wrong. Know this, he says, as the enemy. Then three pictures of how it hides. As fire is covered by smoke. As a mirror is covered by dust. As a baby is covered by the womb. The light is still there. You just can't see it. This enemy, he says, is like a fire that's never satisfied. And he tells you where it lives: in the senses, the mind and the understanding. It uses them to cloud what you know. So he gives an order of strength. The senses are powerful. The mind is higher than the senses. The understanding is higher than the mind. And higher than understanding is the self. Knowing that, steady yourself by the self, and then: jahi shatrum mahabaho kamarupam durasadam. Strike down, mighty-armed one, this enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome. That's chapter three. The action was never the problem. The grasping is.
screen: `BETTER YOUR OWN DHARMA, IMPERFECT.` · `WHAT DRIVES US, AS IF FORCED?` · `DESIRE AND ANGER: THE ENEMY.` · `SMOKE, DUST, THE WOMB.` · then, large: `STRIKE DOWN THE ENEMY CALLED DESIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wipe the mirror. Settle, and breathe. Picture a mirror covered in a fine layer of dust. That's how a strong want sits over what you already know. Now think of one thing you do even though you know better. Name the want underneath it, plainly: I want comfort, I want to be right, I want more. Don't fight it. Just see it for what it is. And each time you breathe out, picture one slow wipe across the glass. Behind the dust, the mirror was always clear. The bell holds the time.
Desire as the enemy. What drives us to act against what we know: desire and anger, hiding like smoke over fire, dust over a mirror.
Your line: know the enemy. Today, when you're about to do the thing you know you shouldn't, stop and name the want out loud. Then choose. Day one hundred seventy.

trapdoor: what you thought: wanting things is bad.
what it means: the grasping kind of desire clouds what you know, like smoke on fire or dust on a mirror. the self behind it is higher and clear.
what a scholar hears: kama is also one of the four aims of life, rightly pursued; here the Gita names its grasping form, born of rajas, as the enemy.

171.title: "Whenever dharma declines, I come" (4.1–4.8)
171.hook: Arjuna asks how his friend could have taught the sun, and Krishna says who he really is
171.howItsDone: Gita 4.7–4.8, yada yada hi dharmasya, is often recited and is read as a classic statement of the avatara, the divine descent; Vaishnava Hindus often read it with the ten avatars of Vishnu in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, desire as the enemy: smoke over fire, dust over a mirror, and chapter three ended. Your line was know the enemy. Did you name a want out loud? Today, chapter four, and Krishna says who he is. Day one hundred seventy-one.

A friend you grew up with mentions, casually, that he taught this same lesson to the sun, ages ago. You'd laugh. Or you'd stare. That's where chapter four begins. Krishna says: this teaching isn't new. I gave it long ago to Vivasvan, the sun. The sun passed it to Manu, father of humankind in Hindu tradition, and Manu to the king Ikshvaku, and down it went, king to king, until over a long time it was lost. Now I'm giving it back to you, because you're my friend. And Arjuna, very reasonably, says: wait. You were born recently. The sun was born long before. How could you have taught him?
screen: `I TAUGHT THIS TO THE SUN.` → `KING TO KING, THEN LOST.` → `BUT YOU WERE BORN RECENTLY.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer: many births have passed, for me and for you, Arjuna. I know them all. You don't. Then he says what he is. Though I am unborn, and my self is imperishable, and I am lord of all beings, I come into being through my own power. And then the promise. In Sanskrit: yada yada hi dharmasya glanir bhavati bharata. Whenever dharma declines. Here's Edwin Arnold's 1885 translation of the two verses: "When Righteousness Declines, O Bharata! when Wickedness Is strong, I rise, from age to age, and take Visible shape, and move a man with men, Succouring the good, thrusting the evil back, And setting Virtue on her seat again." The last words in Sanskrit are sambhavami yuge yuge. I come into being, age after age. This is the root of the idea of the avatara, the descent: the divine coming down into the world in a form, again and again, when things go badly wrong. It's how Vaishnava tradition understands Rama and Krishna, and the list of Vishnu's descents: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf Vamana you met at Onam, and more. Hindu schools read these verses in different ways. Some hear a personal God truly taking a body out of love. Others hear the one reality appearing through its own power, without ever being bound by it. But the promise sounds the same to both. It's not a promise that bad times won't come. It's a promise about what happens when they do. When the wrong grows strong, the good returns. You heard this on Janmashtami, about a baby born in a prison at midnight. Now you've heard it from his own mouth.
screen: `MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.` · `UNBORN, YET I COME INTO BEING.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA DECLINES.` · `AVATARA: THE DESCENT, AGE AFTER AGE.` · then, large: `WHEN THE WRONG GROWS STRONG, HE RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a return. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time when things had gone badly wrong, in your life, your family, the world, and then something good came back that you hadn't expected. A person who showed up. A kindness. A turn. Let it come back clearly. Notice that you couldn't see it coming from inside the dark part. If you pray, you can hold Krishna's promise: age after age, I come. If not, just hold the memory that good has returned before. The bell holds the time.
Whenever dharma declines. Yada yada hi dharmasya. When the right weakens and the wrong grows strong, Krishna says, I come, age after age.
Your line: he returns. Today, when the news or your day feels like the wrong is winning, remember one time the good came back. Day one hundred seventy-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: God shows up to punish bad people.
what it means: whenever the right weakens and the wrong grows strong, the divine takes form, to protect the good and set dharma back on its seat.

172.title: Action without attachment (4.9–4.23)
172.hook: the busiest person in the Gita says his work never touches him, and explains how
172.howItsDone: Some Hindus treat Gita 4.18 as a daily discipline: they work fully, try not to cling to the outcome, and often dedicate a task to God before starting it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna's promise: whenever dharma declines, he comes, age after age. Your line was he returns. Did you notice anything good showing up right when it was needed? Day one hundred seventy-two.

A nurse on a double shift. A grandmother cooking for twenty. Everything is happening around them, and somehow nothing seems to be happening to them. They're working hard, but they aren't grabbing. Then there's the person who does one small task and carries it around all day: did they like it, will it work, what will people say? Same amount of work. Completely different weight. Yesterday Krishna said he comes into the world again and again. Today he says something stranger: all that coming and acting never binds him. And then he tells Arjuna how the same can be true of a person.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENING AROUND THEM.` → `NOTHING HAPPENING TO THEM.` → `SAME WORK, DIFFERENT WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Chapter four, verses nine to twenty-three. Krishna begins with himself. Actions don't stain me, he says, because I have no craving for their fruit. Whoever understands that, he adds, is not bound by action either. Then he admits this is hard. What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused about it. And he gives a riddle, verse eighteen: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people. Read it slowly. Some people sit perfectly still and are churning inside, grabbing at outcomes all day long. That's action hiding in inaction. Others are moving fast, doing a hundred things, and inside they're quiet, not clutching. That's inaction in action. The body can be busy while the grip is loose. The next verses describe that person. They give up clinging to the fruit. They're content, depending on nothing. Even while fully engaged in work, the text says, they do nothing at all, in the sense that matters. They take what comes. They stay even in success and in failure. And verse twenty-three says what happens to their work: it melts away. It doesn't leave the sticky residue that karma usually leaves. Notice what Krishna doesn't say. He doesn't say stop working. Arjuna wanted to walk off the field, and the answer keeps coming back: act. Just act without the hook in you. That's the word today, action without attachment. The work is real. The chain is optional.
screen: `MY ACTIONS DON'T STAIN ME.` · `EVEN THE WISE ARE CONFUSED.` · `INACTION IN ACTION.` · `THE WORK MELTS AWAY.` · then, large: `THE WORK IS REAL. THE CHAIN IS OPTIONAL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one task waiting for you today. Picture yourself doing it, fully, hands and attention on it. Now notice the other thing that comes along: the worry about how it'll turn out, or who will see it. On each out-breath, loosen your grip on that part, just a little. Keep the task. Set down the grabbing. If you pray, you can offer the task to Krishna before you begin it. The bell holds the time.
Action without attachment. Doing the work fully, without clutching at its fruit, so the work doesn't bind you. Inaction in action.
Your line: free while acting. Today, in the middle of something busy, check your grip once. Is your hand on the work, or on the result? Loosen one finger. Day one hundred seventy-two.

173.title: Sacrifice as knowledge (4.24–4.33)
173.hook: the verse many families say before dinner, and a list of a dozen ways to make an offering
173.howItsDone: Some Hindu families, schools and ashrams chant Gita 4.24 (brahmarpanam) as a grace before meals; the idea of offering breath, study and work as yajna shapes daily practice for some.

segments.voice: Yesterday: action without attachment. Your line was free while acting. Did you catch your grip on a result, and loosen a finger? Day one hundred seventy-three.

In some Hindu homes, and in some school dining halls in India, the food is served, everyone waits, and a short Sanskrit verse is chanted before anyone eats. Some children learn it by ear long before they know what it means. Brahmarpanam, it begins. It's a grace before meals, and it comes from today's reading, Gita chapter four, verse twenty-four. What's surprising is what it says. It doesn't thank anyone for the food. It says the food, the eater, the fire and the offering are all one thing. Today: why a verse about fire ended up at the dinner table.
screen: `THE FOOD IS SERVED. EVERYONE WAITS.` → `BRAHMARPANAM.` → `A VERSE AT THE DINNER TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the old Vedic sacrifice, the yajna, a priest pours ghee into a fire, and the fire carries the offering to the gods. Verse twenty-four takes that whole scene and turns it inside out. The act of offering is Brahman, it says. The offering is Brahman. It's poured by Brahman into the fire, which is Brahman. And the one who sees Brahman in the action reaches Brahman. Every part of the ritual is the same reality. So when families chant it over a plate of rice, the meal becomes the fire, the eating becomes the offering. Then Krishna lists the ways people sacrifice, and the list keeps widening. Some offer to the gods. Some offer their senses into the fire of self-control. Some offer their wealth. Some offer austerity, or yoga, or the study of scripture. Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. Even breathing can be a sacrifice. And then verse thirty-three ranks them. Better than any offering of things, Krishna says, is the offering of knowledge, because all action ends in knowledge. The fire has moved inside. What gets burned now isn't ghee. It's ignorance. A few verses later he says it outright: as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns karma to ash. That's the word today, sacrifice as knowledge. Seeing clearly is itself the offering, and the seeing burns.
screen: `THE FIRE, THE GHEE, THE PRIEST.` · `ALL OF IT IS BRAHMAN.` · `EVEN BREATH CAN BE AN OFFERING.` · `THE OFFERING OF KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE BURNS KARMA.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-nine makes breathing an offering, so let's try it. Sit comfortably. Breathe in slowly, and as you do, think: this is given. Breathe out, and think: this is given back. Nothing to fix, nothing to earn. Just the in-breath and the out-breath, each one handed to the other. If your mind wanders, that's fine; bring it back to the next breath. If you pray, you can offer the breath to God. The bell holds the time.
Sacrifice as knowledge. The old fire ritual moved inward: seeing clearly is the highest offering, and the fire it lights burns karma.
Your line: knowledge burns karma. Before one meal today, pause for a single breath and look at the plate as if it were an offering. Day one hundred seventy-three.

fork.reveal: knowledge. verse 33: all action culminates in knowledge, so the offering of knowledge is higher than any offering of things.

original.note: Sanskrit: yajna, sacrifice or offering; the fire ritual of the Vedas, which the Gita widens to all of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: sacrifice means giving something up.
what it means: every act can be an offering, and seeing clearly is the highest one; its fire burns karma.

174.title: Cut the doubt (4.34–4.42)
174.hook: the Gita praises asking questions and warns against doubt in the same breath
174.howItsDone: Many Hindus learn the Gita from a teacher in the spirit of verse 4.34, with respect, questions and service, and the closing call of chapter four, to cut doubt and stand up, is often cited when facing hard decisions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacrifice as knowledge, the fire moved inside. Your line was knowledge burns karma. Did one meal get a breath before it? Day one hundred seventy-four, the end of chapter four.

You know the feeling. It's two in the morning, and you're still deciding. Take the job or don't. Send the text or don't. You've made a list of pros and cons, then another list. Every choice looks wrong from some angle. You're not really thinking anymore; you're circling. That's the Arjuna we met on day one of the Gita, bow on the ground, unable to move. Four chapters later, Krishna closes the chapter with a picture: a sword, and one clean cut. But here's the twist. In the very same passage, he tells Arjuna to ask questions. So which is it?
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING. STILL DECIDING.` → `CIRCLING, NOT THINKING.` → `A SWORD, AND ONE CLEAN CUT.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-four gives the method for learning. Go to those who have seen the truth, Krishna says. Learn by bowing, by questioning, and by serving, and they will teach you. Three Sanskrit words: pranipata, the bow; pariprashna, asking all around a thing; seva, service. So asking is built right into the path. Arjuna himself asks question after question for eighteen chapters, and Krishna never scolds him for it. Then come the promises. Even if you were the worst of wrongdoers, verse thirty-six says, you would cross over all of it on the raft of knowledge. And verse thirty-seven: as a blazing fire turns firewood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all karma to ash. Then the warning. The one without faith, who is always doubting, is lost, verse forty says: for the doubting self there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. So what's the difference between a question and a doubt? A question is moving. It goes somewhere; it wants an answer and will act on one. The doubt Krishna warns about is the kind that circles forever and keeps you from ever standing up. The Sanskrit word for it, samshaya, is the doubt of a mind hung between two sides, never landing on either. And so the final verse of chapter four: cut this doubt in your heart, born of not knowing, with the sword of knowledge. Take refuge in yoga. Stand up, Arjuna. That's today's word: cut the doubt. Keep the questions. Cut the circling.
screen: `BOW, QUESTION, SERVE.` · `THE RAFT OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `THE DOUBTER FINDS NO HAPPINESS.` · `THE SWORD, AND STAND UP.` · then, large: `KEEP THE QUESTIONS. CUT THE CIRCLING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one thing you've been circling. Not the biggest decision of your life; something small that's been going round and round. Breathe slowly. Ask yourself one real question about it, the kind that has an answer. Then, on an out-breath, picture the circling as a thread, and let it be cut. You don't have to decide right now. Just notice the difference between the question and the loop. The bell holds the time.
Cut the doubt. Krishna's last words in chapter four: keep asking real questions, but cut the endless circling with the sword of knowledge, and stand up.
Your line: the sword of knowledge. Today, when you catch yourself circling, ask one question that has an answer, and let it move you. Day one hundred seventy-four.

original.note: Sanskrit: samshaya, doubt; the word Krishna uses for the doubt he tells Arjuna to cut.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means never asking questions.
what it means: ask, and keep asking, but cut the doubt that circles forever and keeps you from standing up.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.36–4.37 (the raft; knowledge burns karma)

175.title: Two paths, one goal (5.1–5.12)
175.hook: Arjuna asks for a straight answer: quit the world, or work in it?
175.howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors both paths: some take formal sannyasa and leave household life, while householders practice karma yoga at home and at work; the lotus leaf of Gita 5.10 is a common image for living in the world untouched by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter four ended with a sword. Cut the doubt; your line was the sword of knowledge. Did a question move you today instead of a loop? Day one hundred seventy-five, the end of the week.
screen: `CUT THE DOUBT — THE SWORD OF KNOWLEDGE.`

segments.voice: Look back at this week. Lead by doing. Know the enemy, desire. He returns, whenever dharma declines. Free while acting. Knowledge burns karma. The sword of knowledge. That's a lot of instruction, and some of it seems to pull two ways. Act, Krishna says, again and again. But also: knowledge is the highest thing, and the wise renounce. So at the top of chapter five, Arjuna does what anyone would do. He says, you've praised giving up action, and you've praised doing action. Just tell me, plainly, which one is better.
screen: `A WEEK OF INSTRUCTIONS.` → `ACT. BUT ALSO, RENOUNCE?` → `JUST TELL ME WHICH ONE.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer, verse two: both lead to the highest good. Renunciation, sannyasa, the path of stepping away from action. And karma yoga, the path of action done without attachment. Both work. Then, since Arjuna asked for a ranking, he gives one: of the two, the yoga of action is better. Why? Verse six: real renunciation is hard to reach without it. And verse three redefines the renouncer anyway. Know as a constant renouncer, Krishna says, the one who neither hates nor craves. The verse says nothing about leaving home. You could be that person with a job and a mortgage. Then verse four: only children, not the wise, talk as if the path of knowledge and the path of yoga were different. Whoever truly stands on one reaches the fruit of both. Verse five says the place the renouncers reach is reached by those who act too. The one who sees them as one, sees. And verse ten gives a picture. The one who acts, offering the actions to Brahman and dropping attachment, is untouched by wrong the way a lotus leaf is untouched by water. The drops sit on the leaf and roll off. The leaf lives in the pond. It's not dry because it left the water. It's dry because the water doesn't cling. That's the word today: two paths. Arjuna wanted a winner. Krishna gave him a ranking, and then a lotus that belongs to both.
screen: `WHICH ONE IS BETTER?` · `BOTH LEAD TO THE HIGHEST GOOD.` · `THE RENOUNCER NEITHER HATES NOR CRAVES.` · `THE LOTUS LEAF IN THE WATER.` · then, large: `TWO PATHS, ONE GOAL.`

segments.voice: A lotus leaf, for two minutes. Sit, and let your hands rest open, palms up, like leaves on a pond. Let the week's thoughts fall on them like drops of water: something someone said, a job left undone, a worry. Don't push them away. Just notice each one land, and let it roll off without soaking in. You stay in the pond. The water doesn't cling. The bell holds the time.
Two paths. Renunciation and the yoga of action. Krishna says both reach the highest good, and the wise see them as one.
Your line: both work. Today, when you're tempted to walk away from something hard, try the lotus instead: stay in the water, and let it roll off. Day one hundred seventy-five.

verse 2: both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the highest good.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you ask Krishna straight out: renounce action, or do action, which is better? what does he answer first?
options: both lead to the highest good.
fork.reveal: both lead to the highest good. only then, because Arjuna asked, does he say the yoga of action is the better of the two.

original.note: Sanskrit: sannyasa, renunciation; also the name for the life stage of the wandering renouncer.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy people leave the world.
what it means: the true renouncer is the one who neither hates nor craves, and that can be someone in the middle of a busy life.

what a scholar hears: 5.4–5 uses sankhya and yoga as names for the paths of knowledge and action and says the wise see them as one; 'padma-patram ivambhasa', like a lotus leaf in water (5.10), is the chapter's picture of acting untouched.
